# Spinning wheel (`spinning_wheel`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/manufacturing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Tools, machines & manufacturing (`manufacturing`)
- Deps: needs textile_fibres; helped by belt_drive
- Core idea: A large wheel turned by hand drives a small horizontal spindle through a cord, so the spindle makes twenty or more turns for one of the wheel. The spinner holds prepared fibre at an angle to the spindle tip and draws it out while the twist runs into it, then moves the hand so the yarn winds on, and repeats. It yields two to three times as much yarn per hour as the hand spindle. The flyer, a U-shaped arm turning round a bobbin that runs slightly slower or faster, twists and winds on at the same time without stopping; a treadle with a crank frees both hands. Spinning stayed the bottleneck of cloth making: one weaver used the yarn of several spinners.
- Pitfalls:
  - Fibre not carded or combed first; lumps make weak, uneven yarn
  - Thinking the wheel replaced the hand spindle at once; wheel yarn was at first softer and was banned for warp in some towns
  - Flyer and bobbin driven at the same speed, so nothing winds on
  - Crediting the treadle to 'Johann Jürgen of Brunswick, 1530'; that is a later legend
- History: china: wheels for reeling and quilling silk from Han times or earlier; spindle wheel for spinning certain by the 11th c., pictured c. 1270; 1313 multi-spindle treadle wheels in Wang Zhen's Nong shu; india: origin there often asserted, but the first unambiguous reference is of 1350 (Isami); Habib argues it arrived from Iran; islamic: by c. 1030 in use; 1237 earliest clear picture, Baghdad (al-Hariri's Maqamat). Place of invention disputed between the Islamic world, India and China; europe: c. 1280 – first evidence (Speyer guild rules of 1298 allow wheel-spun yarn for weft only); c. 1480 flyer and bobbin (Hausbuch; Leonardo); treadle in the 16th c.
- Read:
  - Dieter Kuhn, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol. 5 Part 9: Textile Technology: Spinning and Reeling (1988)
  - Lynn White Jr., Medieval Technology and Social Change (1962)
  - Patricia Baines, Spinning Wheels, Spinners and Spinning (1977)
